content.summary_of_the_paper: In this manuscript, the authors propose a molecular manipulation model, named ChemSpacE, that enables researchers to interact with existing generative models. The model combines HierVAE and MoFlow with SVM to operate on the latent space. The authors demonstrate that the method is model-agnostic and shows the effectiveness and efficiency in several single- and multiple- property constrained optimization benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
* The formulation of the molecular manipulation task is quite interesting and novel.
* The authors provide extensive experimental results and an easy-to-understand demo server.
* The paper is overall well-presented.

Weaknesses:
* Both technical and theoretical contributions are inadequate. Technically, both generating modules and manipulating modules are based on existing models. Theoretically, as the authors mentioned in the conclusion, they don't figure out why the latent space of deep generative models is learned with property boundary, and indeed this is one of the core reasons why previous works have not gone in this direction. This also conflicts with the author's emphasis on interpretability.
* The advantage of using boundary rather than gradient descent for molecular optimization (e.g., https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.01921.pdf) has not been well elucidated. The results of Table 1 cast doubt on the metrics setup, as gradient-based methods have been shown promising in these tasks.
* The entanglement of different properties is quite complicated. It can be said that any property is relevant, as whenever the chemical structure changes, the properties change. In this sense, how can Eq. 9 be used to disentangle the optimization of multiple properties? Is it possible to keep one property changed and other properties unchanged?

Other questions:
* The author's explanation of the boundary in section 3.2 is confusing. In practice, it is not simple to distinguish between drug-like or drug-unlike (this also applies to other properties such as logP, solubility, etc.). How to understand that an absolute boundary that can separate the molecules as good or bad?
* The examples in Fig.5 make no sense. The removal of chirality is formalistic, it does not mean that the bond has no more chirality, and the charge is similar.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good. The paper is overall well-written and organized.

Quality: Good. The performed experiments are extensive.

Novelty: Fair. The proposed modules are mainly based on existing works. 

Reproducibility: Good. The authors provide the codebase.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the setup of this work is interesting and molecular manipulation is a very important application. However, the authors avoid the core issues in the field and the lack of clarity in methodology and metrics setting makes it difficult for the readers to understand the advantages.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a way to explore, and control, the latent spaces produced by different generative model. The idea is that there is a (linear) separation, in the latent space, $z$, between molecules that have high and low values for particular properties. Then moving in the direction of the normal vector of the separating hyperplane takes us from low to high property values. The paper uses this to manipulate in a systematic and controlled manner the properties of a given molecule. The method presented there can be used over any latent space without any need to retraining.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: To my understanding moving along the normal vector of the hyperplane that separates molecules to two different classes is equivalent to having the linear property predictor $f(g(z))=\eta^{\text{T}} z$. Note that the gradient of that property predictor with respect to $z$ is $\eta$ thus to maximize a desired property of a given molecule we simply need to move from $z$ to $z+\eta$. This process is, at least to my understanding, pretty much the same thing that happens when one does gradient-based property optimization using some more general property predictor $f(g(z))$. Thus it seems to me that the basic difference of the method proposed here from any gradient-based property optimization is the simplification of the property predictor and its replacement with a linear function. Other than that the two approaches are doing essentially the same thing. Both move along the gradient of a more or less complex property predictor function. The rate with which they move along the gradient direction should basically determine whether there is a monotonic, or not, change. A large movement on the direction of the gradient means that one might overshoot the local maximum. This rate is at the end the hyperparameter that controls to a large extend the success rate measures. Related to that is the number of oracle calls
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper reads rather easily, however a number of important details are missing or at least I did not find them in the manuscript. Probably the most important is how the rate of change, the $\alpha$, is set of the chemical space exploration method but also for the gradient-based method. In relation to that a discussion on the similarities of the two approaches with an emphasis of how their respective gradients behave would have been more than useful. The gradient of the Chemical Space Exploration method is constant through out the latent space, will this of the proxies used in optimization based methods would vary considerably depending to where we are in the search space. In relation to that it is not clear what happens when we take one of the $k$ manipulation steps in the first set of experiments. There in table 2, we see that the optimization based approach does 120k calls to the oracle while the chemical exploration method makes 300 to 400 calls. Bellow I discuss a number of additional issues mostly with respect to the evaluation. 

The paper explores two evaluation settings: molecule manipulation and molecule optimization in the latent space. 

Under molecule manipulation we are given some starting molecule and we want to manipulate one or more properties 
over a sequence of manipulation steps; each manipulation steps produces a molecule. A succesful manipulation 
step-sequence will produce monotonic changes in the property values. To evaluate manipulation quality the paper
introduces the strict and relaxed success rates (SSR/RSR). In the SSR measure a manipulation sequence is considered
successful only if all sequence steps have produced molecules with monotonically changing properties, monotonically 
decreasing similarities with respect to the initial molecule and molecules that are different from the initial molecule. 

A natural baseline for the molecule manipulation is gradient-based search in the latent space. According to the results
of property manipulation (Table 1) the chemical space explolarion method with MoFlow has a considerable higher SSR than 
the gradient-based. One important hyperparameter in the gradient-based search is the step one takes at each gradient step
and I am not sure I found information on that in the text. Depending on the size of the step one might have trivially low
or trivially high SSR (large step, small step, respectively). The same role is also played by the $\alpha$ parameter of 
the Chemical Space Exploration. This step-size makes the comparison between the Chemical Space Exploration and the gradient-based 
property optimization not obvious.

An additional useful information would be the property change, and similarity change, that occured by the k steps, though this is 
given in the follow-up evaluation of property evaluation. 

Why there is no gradient-based search for HierVAE or as a matter of fact for JT-VAE? From my understanind Chemical Space Exploration 
is a kind of meta-method and could be applied for any method that provides a latent space. 

In the molecule optimization setting we are given an initial molecule and we want to improve one or more properties while having
at least $\delta$ similarity with the original molecule. Evaluation measures here include the property improvement, the similarity
of the final and starting molecules, and the percentage of succesfully optimized molecules within the desired $\delta$ similarity
threshold. Looking at the results in Table 3, I am not sure I can say I see an important difference between MoFlow and Chemical Space 
Exploration. All performance values are within the standard deviation/error. 

Detail, the acronyms of the methods that are evaluated under the molecule optimization task are not defined until the related work 
section. If I am not mistaken JT-VAE is also doing gradient based optimization? If yes, it could have also been included in the 
property manipulation section.

I did not find a more detailed description of how the class boundaries are defined for each property, I guess some threshold value 
is defined, a number of molecules are encoded in the latent space, and then a linear model is established there.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a method for manipulating the latent space for molecule generation. It seems that the method is not very different from other optimization based methods that rely on a proxy of a property predictor. The main difference here is that the property predictor is a linear function here, whereas in classical property optimization works such a property predictor is a highly non-linear function. The behavior of these two versions of property manipulation hinges a lot on the nature of the linear vs non-linear property predictors as well as on the change of rate, the $\alpha$, something which is not really discussed in the paper. In addition there are a lot of important details that are missing or not discussed.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new method to steer the latent space of generative models to manipulate the target property. The model identifies the directions in the latent space and applies a k consecutive step that leads to the improvement of the target property. Unlike the existing models, it does not require fine-tuning for every new target property and the experimental result shows improvement over the Bayesian optimization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The method can be integrated into any existing generative models with the latent space and does not require retraining for each new target property as bayesian optimization does. Also, this method provides a tool for us to look at in deep how the properties of a molecule and the structure of the molecule (latent space) are related. 
Weakness: even though works really well, the proposed assumption seems to me a bit oversimplified and could fail when we consider real-world cases.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow, and the proposed idea seems to be novel, and includes most of the details to reproduce the work.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is very well written which makes it easy to follow. I have some minor confusions that may need to be clarified: 

1) I wonder if it really works for multiple property manipulation, is the assumption that molecules with similar properties are close in the latent space still holds? also even for a single property, is it really true that for all the properties, the molecule with similar properties is mapped to close points in the latent space?

2) I am still not very sure about the latent cluster assumption, as molecules live in discrete space and molecules have this Activity cliff where small changes in the structure could lead to a big change in the properties. I feel like this assumption could hold for some properties but could also not hold when we consider some other properties. 

3) In section 3.3 when discussing manipulating multiple properties, the paper points out that one needs to first identify disentangled properties, and then modify those disentangled and positively correlated ones, how to identify the disentangled properties? I feel like most of the properties are entangled in some way. 

4) I was wondering if figure 2 is cherry-picked or generalizable for all the molecules in the dataset used here.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed to traverse the latent space learned by a pre-trained molecule generative model to optimize certain molecular properties. The mapping from the latent space to the property values is parameterized by a linear model, which is learned before traversing the latent space. To evaluate the quality of the traversal, the paper proposed SSR and RSR to measure the percentage of traversals with monotonically changing property values. The paper demonstrated that the model can achieve much higher SSR and RSR than baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper presented an interesting and novel formulation of the molecular space exploration problem by measuring the percentages of monotonically changing paths. Having such an interactive system would make machine-learning-based methods more accessible to domain experts.
- The proposed method was compared with random/largest range/gradient-based baselines and achieved dominant performance.

Weaknesses:
- On the methodology side, the contribution of this paper is incremental. 
   - Many existing work have discussed using the latent space for molecular optimization.
   - Equation (9) is not justified. The paper did not explain why using a linear combination of directions would be helpful here.
   - The assumption made in this paper, i.e., having a global linear relationship between the latent space and property value, is too strong. This can be improved by either using a local linear model or enforcing such constraint when learning a latent space during pre-training.
Whether we should use SSR as the primary metric is debatable. The main task here is to obtain a higher property value. It’s acceptable to see the property value drop by 20% and then increase by 40%. SSR/RSR can be used as a secondary metric.
- The experiments lack key results on property value improvement for difficult property values such as DRD2, JNK3, and GSK3B. Tables 3 and 7 are not sufficient since plogp and qed are relatively easy properties.
- Whether this method is interpretable is debatable. The proposed method showed gradual changes in structure, but it is not sufficient to say that such a method is interpretable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is mostly clear. Section 3.2 did not explain how to learn the normal vector(s), and did not explain what the circled dot symbol in Equation 9 meant.
- Quality and novelty are commented on in Strength And Weaknesses.
- Reproducibility should be good with the accompanying code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper proposed to use a linear model to optimize molecules in the latent space, but it did not present a solid contribution due to the issues listed above.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
